title: Does private lending in emerging markets deliver competitive returns? Evidence suggests it does
gist: A World Bank/IFC paper using 4,109 IFC loans (~$115 billion, 127 countries, 1992-2024) finds emerging-market private lending earns returns competitive with public benchmarks, outperforming the CEMBI and US Treasuries post-GFC, with fragile-state loans showing higher defaults but statistically similar returns.

insights.claim: A study of 4,109 IFC loans totaling about $115 billion across 127 countries from 1992 to 2024 finds private lending in emerging and developing economies delivers returns competitive with widely used public market benchmarks.
insights.so_what: Supports allocating to EM private credit, a segment investors often avoid on perceived risk.
insights.quote: private lending in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs) can deliver returns competitive with widely used public market benchmarks.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Since 2012, IFC's loan portfolio outperformed the CEMBI Broad Diversified EM corporate bond index with a public market equivalent (PME) of 1.02 and US Treasuries with a PME of 1.10, rising to 1.05 and 1.14 over the last five years.
insights.so_what: Post-GFC EM direct lending has beaten both EM corporate bonds and Treasuries on a cash-flow-matched basis.
insights.quote: The IFC loan portfolio outperformed both the CEMBI Broad Diversified emerging-market corporate bond index (PME of 1.02) and US Treasuries (PME of 1.10).
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Over 2002-2024, IFC's loan portfolio earned a PME of 0.98 against the CEMBI and 1.07 against Treasuries, with the slight CEMBI underperformance driven by GFC-era vintages that absorbed elevated defaults.
insights.so_what: Full-cycle EM loan returns roughly match EM bonds, so the illiquidity premium is not always earned.
insights.quote: The portfolio earned a PME of 0.98 against the CEMBI and 1.07 against Treasuries.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: IFC loan returns track the global credit cycle: loans originated just before the 2008 crisis returned $0.81 against the corporate bond benchmark, while loans originated in recovery years such as 2021 outperformed by 13%.
insights.so_what: Vintage timing matters: deploying EM private credit in recovery years has paid off, late-cycle lending has not.
insights.quote: Loans originated just before the 2008 crisis returned $0.81 against the corporate bond benchmark — the weakest vintage
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The study is distinctive in analyzing privately issued direct loans to firms rather than public corporate bonds, since direct loans make up much of corporate financing in developing countries.
insights.so_what: Provides rare loan-level evidence for an opaque asset class.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: In fragile and conflict-affected situations and IDA-eligible countries, IFC loan default rates are higher but benchmarked returns are statistically indistinguishable from the overall portfolio average.
insights.so_what: Frontier-market credit risk appears adequately priced, challenging blanket avoidance by investors.
insights.quote: Default rates are higher in these environments, but benchmarked returns are statistically indistinguishable from the overall portfolio average.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Among IFC loans in fragile settings, 11.3% fall below a PME of 0.8 versus 9.5% elsewhere and 13.5% exceed 1.2 versus 10.6%, so FCS returns are slightly more dispersed but the distributions overlap closely.
insights.so_what: Fragile-state lending adds tail dispersion on both sides rather than systematically lower returns.
insights.quote: 11.3 percent fall below a PME of 0.8 against 9.5 percent elsewhere, and 13.5 percent exceed 1.2 against 10.6 percent
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The sample excludes blended-finance loans, so the authors caution the results do not show private capital will flow to fragile and low-income markets at scale without concessional first-loss support.
insights.so_what: IFC's preferred-creditor status and selection may not be replicable by purely private lenders.
insights.quote: These results should not be interpreted as evidence that private capital will flow to fragile and low-income markets at scale without concessional support.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Investors often assume emerging-market lending carries higher risk without higher returns, and such perceptions shape whether capital reaches firms that drive growth and jobs.
insights.so_what: A perception gap may leave EM credit structurally underpriced relative to realized returns.
insights.quote: Investors often assume that lending in emerging markets carries higher risk without higher returns.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The authors call for investors, DFIs and policymakers to improve market data and transparency so investors can distinguish perceived risk from actual risk, potentially unlocking significantly more private capital.
insights.so_what: Better data releases (e.g., loan-level DFI data) could catalyze inflows into EM private credit.
insights.quote: so that investors can better distinguish perceived risk from actual risk.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
